summary: Defines a RADIUS Attributes suboption that lets a network element pass identification and authorization attributes it got during RADIUS authentication to a DHCP server through the relay agent information option.

plainLanguage.summary: The doorman who checked your ID passes a note about you to the person who hands out room numbers.

subtitle: How a network access device hands RADIUS authorization attributes to a DHCP server through the relay agent.

tldr.problem: A switch or access point may learn authorization attributes about a user from a RADIUS server, but the DHCP server that assigns the user's configuration never sees them.
tldr.mechanism: The relay agent adds a RADIUS Attributes suboption (code 7) to the DHCP Relay Agent Information option, carrying the RADIUS attributes encoded as RFC 2865 specifies. The DHCP server reads them when choosing configuration parameters.
tldr.outcome: DHCP configuration can follow what RADIUS authorized. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9445.

today: RFC 4014 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9445. Check that update for the current rules.

sections.title: Passing RADIUS Attributes to DHCP
sections.content:
RFC 4014 defines a RADIUS Attributes suboption for the DHCP Relay Agent Information option. It gives a Network Access Server (NAS) a way to pass attributes it obtained from a RADIUS server on to a DHCP server.

The motivating case is IEEE 802.1X. A device first exchanges credentials with a NAS such as a switch or a wireless access point. The NAS sends them to a RADIUS server, which answers with an Access-Accept or an Access-Reject. The NAS then allows or denies network access. The suboption is not limited to 802.1X, though. It can carry RADIUS attributes the relay agent obtained for any reason.
sections.plainLanguage: A gatekeeper checks who you are and learns some things about you. This RFC lets the gatekeeper pass those notes on to whoever assigns your network settings.

sections.title: Where the Pieces Fit and Where It Applies
sections.content:
The access device does two jobs. It acts as the IEEE 802.1X Authenticator and as a DHCP relay agent. When authentication succeeds, the RADIUS Access-Accept gives the NAS attributes for service authorizations, and the NAS stores them locally. Later, when it relays DHCP messages from the device, it adds those attributes in a RADIUS Attributes suboption.

The scope is deliberately narrow. Robust interoperability is only guaranteed when the RADIUS service lives in the same scope as the DHCP service, that is, within a single, localized administrative domain. Global interoperability across administrative domains is not required.

The RFC also says its use of MUST and SHOULD applies only to RADIUS clients and servers that implement this optional feature. It does not change the base RADIUS specifications such as RFC 2865.
sections.plainLanguage: The note only works inside one building's rules. The gatekeeper and the room-number person have to work for the same place.

sections.title: The Suboption Format
sections.content:
The suboption is laid out as a code, a length and the attributes. The sub-option code is 7, the length byte is N, and the following octets o1 to oN hold the RADIUS attributes. They are encoded according to the encoding rules in RFC 2865, so each one is a Type-Length-Value tuple.

Space in the suboption is limited. The relay agent truncates the RADIUS attributes to make them fit.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small envelope with a label saying what kind of note it is, how long the note is, and then the note itself. If the note is too long, the doorman cuts it short.

sections.title: What the Relay Agent and Server Do
sections.content:
When the relay agent gets a DHCP message from a client, it MAY append a Relay Agent Information option containing the RADIUS Attributes suboption. The suboption MUST only contain attributes from the RADIUS Access-Accept message, and the agent MUST NOT add more than one per message. If available, the agent MUST include User-Name and Framed-Pool.

To avoid entangling address allocation and other state between the RADIUS and DHCP servers, the agent SHOULD include only the attributes in a short list: User-Name (1), Service-Type (6), Vendor-Specific (26), Session-Timeout (27), Framed-Pool (88) and Framed-IPv6-Pool (100).

The DHCP server extracts the suboption contents and uses them in selecting configuration parameters for the client. It SHOULD ignore any attributes outside that list, because using others might cause side effects the existing RADIUS specifications did not anticipate. DHCP clients never see the suboption, since relay agent options only travel between relay agents and the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorman attaches the note only for a short list of useful facts, like your name and which group of rooms you belong to. The room-number person ignores anything else, and you never even see the note.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The Relay Agent option depends on a trusted relationship between the relay agent and the DHCP server, as RFC 3046 describes. A perimeter defense that blocks these options unless the relay agent is trusted can prevent fraudulent ones. The RFC says a deeper defense, using the authentication suboption for relay agent options or IPsec, SHOULD be deployed as well. It also points to RFC 3118 for DHCP message authentication and to section 7 of RFC 2131 for potential attacks.

On the IANA side, the value 7 was assigned as the suboption code. The document defines no new namespaces or other constants for IANA to maintain.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the room-number person trusts these notes, you must make sure nobody can slip in a fake one. Locks at the door and a sealed envelope help.
